title: Browser With 10 LRU Tabs
statement:
Design a browser in which only a limited number of tabs can stay open. When a new tab is opened while the browser is full, the **least recently used** tab is closed automatically. The original interview version allowed 10 open tabs; here the limit is a parameter `C`.

Each tab has a string id. The browser supports two operations:

- `open id`: use the tab `id`. If a tab with this id is already open, it simply becomes the most recently used tab and nothing is closed. Otherwise a new tab is opened as the most recently used one; if that would make more than `C` tabs, the least recently used tab is closed first.
- `list`: report the open tabs.

For every `open` operation print the id of the tab that was closed by it, or `none` if no tab was closed. For every `list` operation print the open tabs from the most recently used to the least recently used, separated by spaces, or `empty` if no tab is open.

**Follow-up:** the interviewer first asked to explain and implement the internal working of a `HashMap`, and to explain the data structure, logic and time complexity of the browser. Aim for O(1) per `open`: a hash map combined with a doubly linked list.
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `n` and `C`.
Each of the next `n` lines is either `open id` or `list`.
outputFormat: Print one line per operation, in order: for `open` the id of the closed tab or `none`; for `list` the open tabs from most to least recently used, or `empty`.
constraints: `id` is a non-empty string of at most 8 lowercase letters and digits

complexity.time: O(1) per open, O(C) per list

hints: You need to find a tab by id quickly and also know which tab is the least recently used. Think about which structures give each of those in O(1).
A hash map from id to a node in a doubly linked list ordered by recency lets you move a node to the front and drop the tail in O(1).
In Python or JavaScript, an ordered dictionary or `Map` (which preserves insertion order) can play the role of both.
